content.intro: This lesson covers Creating and Opening Workbooks as part of Excel Interface and Workbook Fundamentals. It follows the attached Excel curriculum, with an emphasis on small examples and verification.
content.why_it_matters: Creating and Opening Workbooks establishes the workbook structure and data-quality habits that later formulas and reports depend on. A clear layout reduces avoidable editing mistakes and makes the workbook easier for another person to understand. File-format note: CSV stores a single flat text table and does not preserve workbook features such as multiple sheets, formatting, charts or formulas as workbook objects. Verify data types, delimiters and leading zeros after conversion.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Creating and Opening Workbooks focuses on the following parts of the supplied syllabus: Blank workbooks and templates; Opening existing workbooks; Opening CSV and text files; Working with recent files. Keep the underlying source data visible and make each assumption explicit.

content_blocks.code: Raw input → organized worksheet/table → calculation or analysis → validated output
content_blocks.expected_output: A basic worksheet workflow separates raw inputs from calculations and outputs, then checks the result against the source.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a copy of the workbook; keep clear headers, avoid blank rows inside tables, and compare row counts/totals before and after a structural edit.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Work in a duplicate workbook or a scratch sheet. Restore the input range and formula/code to the original state, clear filters or selections, then rerun the same test cases. Record expected and actual behavior rather than assuming a successful result.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a small, known dataset for creating and opening workbooks. Apply the example above, compute or inspect at least one result independently, then deliberately try a blank, duplicate, boundary, or not-found case where relevant.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small worksheet or workbook section that demonstrates creating and opening workbooks. Use clear headers, label units and assumptions, and capture expected versus actual output for a normal case and an edge case. Where the concept requires a specialized Excel feature, first verify that feature is available in your Excel edition.

content.task: Build or inspect an Excel example that demonstrates creating and opening workbooks; use the example to verify one normal and one edge case, and write down any version or tool dependency.
task_acceptance_criteria: The worksheet/workflow uses a clear, labeled source range and explicit assumptions.
The learner records an expected output and independently compares it with the actual result.
At least one relevant edge case is checked; data and formula errors are not silently concealed.
The workbook is saved as a copy and compatibility/security/accessibility notes are followed where relevant.
hints: Reduce the problem to a small range with known values before scaling it up.
Inspect cell values and formulas, not only displayed formatting; verify data types, references and range boundaries.
Compare expected versus actual results and check the Microsoft documentation for version-specific functions or tools.
content.expected_output: A basic worksheet workflow separates raw inputs from calculations and outputs, then checks the result against the source.
common_mistakes: Assuming the displayed format is the same as the stored value or data type.
Using an incorrect range boundary, a mismatched lookup key, or an unverified assumption.
Trusting a result without comparing it with a known calculation or checking a failure/edge case.
